pharm: Binds hydroxyapatite in bone and inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, reducing bone turnover and increasing bone mineral density
quick: Delayed-release 35 mg once weekly after breakfast (immediate-release: 5 mg daily, 35 mg weekly, or 150 mg monthly)
Delayed-release: immediately after breakfast; immediate-release: 30 min before first food/drink
Insufficient data; discontinue when pregnancy is recognized (potential fetal skeletal harm)
Not recommended; presence in human milk unknown
Not recommended if CrCl below 30 mL/min
No specific adjustment; not hepatically metabolized
No specific interaction; alcohol may worsen GI irritation
Serum calcium, vitamin D status, dental health, BMD
summary: Risedronate sodium is a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate that inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. The delayed-release tablet is indicated for treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis at 35 mg once weekly taken immediately after breakfast; immediate-release tablets are used for osteoporosis (prevention/treatment), glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, and Paget disease. Correct hypocalcemia before starting, take with water while staying upright, and reassess the need for continued therapy after 3 to 5 years.
indications: Treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women (reduces vertebral and nonvertebral osteoporosis-related fractures)
Immediate-release also used for prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, osteoporosis in men, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, and Paget disease of bone (per immediate-release labeling)

dosage.d: One 35 mg delayed-release tablet orally once weekly
dosage.n: Take in the morning immediately following breakfast with at least 4 ounces of plain water

dosage.d: 5 mg daily, or 35 mg once weekly, or 150 mg once monthly
dosage.n: Take at least 30 minutes before the first food or drink of the day (per immediate-release labeling)

dosage.t: 2-month course; retreatment after follow-up if needed

dosage.n: Risedronate is not recommended in severe renal impairment

admin: Delayed-release: take in the morning immediately following breakfast (not fasting - higher risk of abdominal pain if taken fasting)
Swallow whole, upright, with at least 4 ounces of plain water; do not chew, cut, or crush
Avoid lying down for at least 30 minutes after the dose
Take supplemental calcium and vitamin D if dietary intake is inadequate
Take calcium, antacids, magnesium-based supplements/laxatives, and iron preparations at a different time of day (they impair absorption)
Do not co-administer with the same active ingredient (e.g. Actonel)
moa: Risedronate has an affinity for hydroxyapatite crystals in bone and acts as an antiresorptive agent. At the cellular level it inhibits osteoclasts; the osteoclasts adhere normally to the bone surface but show reduced active resorption (lack of ruffled border). Histomorphometry showed that risedronate reduces bone turnover (activation frequency) and bone resorption at remodeling sites.

absolute: Abnormalities of the esophagus that delay esophageal emptying (e.g. stricture or achalasia)
Inability to stand or sit upright for at least 30 minutes
Known hypersensitivity to any component (angioedema, generalized rash, bullous skin reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis reported)
relative: Active upper GI disease (Barrett esophagus, dysphagia, esophageal disease, gastritis, duodenitis, ulcers)
Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) - not recommended
Invasive dental procedures / poor oral health (osteonecrosis of the jaw risk)
monitor: Serum calcium and vitamin D status (correct hypocalcemia before starting)
Upper GI symptoms (dysphagia, odynophagia, retrosternal pain, new/worsening heartburn)
New thigh or groin pain (atypical femur fracture)

preg: Available data on use of risedronate in pregnant women are insufficient to inform a drug-associated risk. Discontinue risedronate when pregnancy is recognized. In animal studies, risedronate decreased neonatal survival and body weight, caused a low incidence of cleft palate and delayed skeletal ossification, and periparturient maternal hypocalcemia. Because bisphosphonates are incorporated into bone and released over weeks to years, there is a potential risk of fetal skeletal harm if a woman becomes pregnant after completing therapy.
lact: There are no data on the presence of risedronate in human milk, effects on the breastfed infant, or effects on milk production. Use during breastfeeding is not recommended; weigh the benefits against potential risk.
renal: Risedronate is not recommended for use in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min). No dosage adjustment is needed for mild to moderate impairment per labeling.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is needed; there is no evidence of systemic metabolism of risedronate and it does not induce or inhibit hepatic microsomal enzymes.

moderate: Calcium supplements / antacids - reduce risedronate bioavailability (about 38%); separate dosing times
Magnesium-based supplements/laxatives and iron preparations - interfere with absorption; separate dosing

H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors - may cause faster release from delayed-release tablets and increase exposure (esomeprazole increased Cmax 60%, AUC 22%); concomitant use not recommended with delayed-release
Aspirin / NSAIDs - may increase upper GI adverse reactions
interactions.food: Food markedly affects absorption; delayed-release taken after breakfast, immediate-release taken fasting before first food/drink
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described; alcohol may aggravate GI irritation
interactions.diagnostics: May affect bone-imaging agents; correct/monitor serum calcium

serious: Esophagitis, esophageal ulcers/erosions, occasionally with bleeding; rarely stricture or perforation
Severe bone, joint, or muscle pain
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions: angioedema, generalized rash, bullous skin reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis
emergency: Esophageal perforation or severe GI bleeding

monitoring: Serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D (correct deficiency before starting)
Renal function (avoid if CrCl below 30 mL/min)
Dental/oral health, especially before invasive dental procedures
Bone mineral density and periodic re-evaluation of need for continued therapy (after 3-5 years for low-risk patients)
counsel: Take the weekly delayed-release tablet right after breakfast with a full glass (at least 4 oz) of plain water, and stay upright for 30 minutes
Do not chew, cut, or crush the tablet
Stop the medicine and seek care for difficulty or pain on swallowing, chest pain, or new/worsening heartburn
Take calcium, iron, antacids, and magnesium products at a different time of day
Tell your dentist you take this medicine, and report new thigh or groin pain
pk: Antiresorptive effect develops over weeks; fracture-risk reduction over months
Tmax about 3 hours for the delayed-release tablet taken before a meal
Long terminal elimination from bone (bisphosphonates released over weeks to years); plasma clearance ~122 mL/min
Prolonged skeletal retention; effects persist after stopping
pearls: Oral bioavailability is very low (~0.6%) and highly affected by food and divalent cations - dosing instructions are critical
The delayed-release 35 mg weekly tablet is taken immediately after breakfast, unlike immediate-release tablets which are taken fasting before the first food or drink
Correct hypocalcemia and ensure adequate vitamin D before starting
Watch for osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures with long-term use; consider a drug holiday after 3-5 years in low-risk patients
Separate calcium, iron, antacids, and magnesium products from the dose; PPIs/H2 blockers are not recommended with the delayed-release formulation
missed: If a once-weekly dose is missed, take one tablet on the morning after you remember, then return to taking one tablet once a week on your originally scheduled day. Do not take two tablets on the same day.
overdose: Substantial overdose may cause decreases in serum calcium and phosphorus and signs/symptoms of hypocalcemia. Milk or calcium-containing antacids may bind immediate-release risedronate to reduce absorption (impact on delayed-release not evaluated); gastric lavage may be considered to remove unabsorbed drug. Treat hypocalcemia with standard measures including intravenous calcium to restore physiologic ionized calcium.
